A complete candidate would preserve the founder's developmental instruction through ordinary genome replication. Genetic variation would change the rule; differential reproduction would retain the variants that reconstruct useful function.

This makes DNA inheritance plus reproductive selection the feedback-to-memory interface, without requiring every useful chemical reaction to produce a separate genetic recording event.

That is a meaningful simplification, but it exposes three indispensable physical requirements.

First, reproductive descendants must inherit the complete developmental programme rather than only a terminally differentiated worker state.

Second, a newly established lineage must be able to regenerate its indispensable specialists. In the previous three-role bootstrap calculation, the modelled ordered differentiation scheme succeeds with probability approximately 0.859, against 2/9 for three independent random assignments. If a failed initial bootstrap is unrecoverable, this difference affects whether the lineage can persist.

Third, the metabolites supporting reproduction must predominantly come from the newly regenerated lineage. Cell adhesion is not sufficient by itself: diffusible nutrients can still reach unrelated cells. Experimental work on yeast sucrose digestion illustrates this public-good problem, while newer programmable adhesion and cross-feeding systems demonstrate useful but incomplete components.

### The strongest remaining physical obstruction

The central difficulty is closing the material-credit loop while retaining a renewable reproductive lineage.

If the founder consumes metabolites provided by unrelated cells, growth no longer certifies its own developmental instructions. If all daughters become terminal specialists, the genetic instruction may cease to produce independently viable founders. If the founder can reproduce indefinitely without specialist function, selection has little reason to retain the specialists.

The physical system needs a genuinely reproductive founder population whose continued expansion depends on function reconstructed by its own descendants.

This conjunction is not established by the cited experiments.
